title.en: Measuring a tower from the ground

text.en: Surveyors measure mountains and towers using only an angle and a distance on the ground. Trigonometry makes that possible.

The line of sight is the line from the eye of the observer to the object being viewed.
The angle of elevation is the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal when you look up at an object.
The angle of depression is the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal when you look down at an object.
Step one: draw a clear figure and mark the right triangle. Step two: mark the known lengths and angles.
Step three: choose the ratio that connects the known side and the unknown side. Use tan when height and ground distance are involved.
Example: from a point 20 m from a tower's foot, the angle of elevation of the top is 60 degrees. Height = 20 tan 60 = 20 root 3 m.
Remember that the angle of depression from a point equals the angle of elevation from the object below, because of alternate angles.
Add the observer's eye height when the problem says so, and give the answer with units.

problem.en: A tower stands on level ground. From a point 30 m away, the angle of elevation of the top is 30 degrees. Find the height.

prompt.en: Explain angle of elevation and depression and how to start a problem.

requiredIdeas.en: Draw and mark the right triangle

commonMisconceptions.en: Measuring the angle from the vertical

points.en: Angle of elevation: line of sight above the horizontal; depression: below it.
Draw the right triangle and choose the correct ratio.
Typical use: height = distance x tan(angle).
